I should have answer'd Yrs sooner, had not George wrote you Word that I agree to ye Gardiner's proposals & hope in a Day or two to have notice of his coming, for I shd be glad to see him Settled here, before I repair to London to begin ye Acting Season - I hope he has a good Character in his Neighborhood, for he will be left in trust of Every thing, house, Garden Workmen &c &c - you must likewise be so good to say what Expences I am to be at for his Journey, tho as I agree to his wages wch are high (I think that he might have bore his own Expences to Town - however that I leave to you - We shall have no occasion for a Laundry Maid, so we shall spare you that trouble, for my Wife has alter'd that scheme, at least for a time - but if you shd know of two Maids between this & next Spring, one for Laundry & ye other for a Dairy & the Chickens wch are prime in their Way, we shd be greatly oblig'd to You, if You would give us Notice of them, & secure them for Us - as to Mrs I should be proud & pleas'd to Serve any of her family, as I did one of her Daughters before - but to obtain a Place yt would be fit for her to accept, would take up Some time & Enquiry, for the People of fashion are all out of Town, & Those I am immediatly intimate wth are provided with favourites, wch I neither can, or indeed would chuse to remove - I shall be willing to Say Every thing favourable & kind of ye Young Lady, if I should have an opportunity, or if my good opinion will be Ever Serviceable to her, she may command Me at all times We were indeed most happy at Windham's, all mirth, Joy, Love Elegance & what not. he desird his best wishes to you very affecty - He seems thoughtfull at times, greatly so, & I don't absolutely like his Looks & Cough - I write this in great hurry for I have Compy wth Me. I have Enclos'd (as I have a frank) Some of our periodical Papers - I will not answer for
their Superlative Merit, such as they are you are wellcome to - We send our Love to you all
& I am Yrs Ever
D Garrick
Hampton
Wednesday Morng

After I had wrote to Your Lordp I went to Chiswick to call upon my wife to go to Hampton - Lady Burlington desir'd to see Me before I set off, I went into her Room, & she told Me with tears, that she had not slept one Wink all Night wth reflecting upon our conversation - she then Said, that she must desire me to do for her, what she had several times intended to ask me, wch was, to talk wth Your Lordp from her, & beg to know, wt may have been ye Cause of yr Lordships Coolness & Gravity of late; that she cannot charge herself with ye least Neglect or Unkindness, & that Your Behavior which is so reserv'd, afflicts her so sensibly that she must intreat to know ye Reason for it makes her Life miserable - this is ye thing I could have wish'd, & as she has desir'd that you may not know of her Ladp's & my conversation, Nothing could have happen'd so luckily - she says my talking to her has oblig'd her beyond Measure, & indeed I never saw Such a Change from ye Severe, to ye Good & tender. She is greatly allarm'd, & gets me as often as she can into a Corner for advice, & I am to lye there to Night again in order to have my Instructions of What I am to say to Yr Lordship - now indeed is ye time to fix Matters upon such a footing, that No uneasiness shall Enter again into ye family; I cannot say that I have been so pleas'd & satisfy'd a long time; & Yr Lordp may be assur'd that I have acted with all ye Prudence & delicacy, so nice an affair requires, & let me likewise say, with that firmness & regard to both, that unless the Devil steps in between, (and I flatter myself that he is shut out at present) Good, real Good must be ye Consequence. pray let me know when I may see Yr Lordp, for Ly Burlington has desir'd that I will see You as soon as I can; I suppose Tuesday or Wednesday Morng will be ye farthest. Mrs Garrick sends her Duty & I am
as in duty bound Yr Lordship's most faithful & Obedt Sert
D Garrick.
PS. Yr Lordp must take no Notice of this, till I see you; but this was unnecessary - Yr Lordp has now time to consider what is further to be done.
My Lord.

Yesterday, & not before, I had the critical Tete a tete with her almost unintelligible Ladyship: We walk'd into ye Garden togeather & she began wth asking Me, whether yr Lordship had said anything more of Your Grievances - No Madam (said I) his Lp talk'd no more of that affair; I indeed Spoke to him & told him I was glad to see that his Lordp seem'd to be chearfuller than Some time ago. Your answer was to Me - While her Ladyp is pleas'd to be kind I shall return it, & live wth her, (if she pleases) as We Us'd to do before these Bickerings, but I cannot, & ought not, to pass my Life in gloom & with unkind treatment: it is very odd said she; - but I saw her struck & much touch'd & this Subject dropt - I wanted to introduce the grand affair, wch I did by asking her, when you was to return, She said, she did not know, that she had ask'd Ly Hartn, but she could not tell - I suppose says I, this new Scheme of another house near Uffington is taking place & his Lp is there - oh No Says She, I believe he is still at Chatsworth - then I came in to ye Matter - I could not help laughing at my Lord (said I) for thinking of another house in that cursed Country, & said to Him how can Yr Lordp think of any place when You may have Londesburgh - how so Mr David cri'd his Lordp? Why I have heard My Lady Burlington say that she Wonder'd how you could go there when you might have Londesburgh; if Lady B - would Chuse it to be so (reply'd yr Lp) she certainly would have Spoke of it - why have I not? (interrupted ye Lady) Several & Several times? you have heard me, have you not? I don't remember Your Saying this to Ld H: Madm, I recollect Something of yr Saying this to Ly Hart. but that was in a careless Way -

I mean says she Every thing I say, & I shd think what is said to One is said to Both - I am very sorry (said I) there is ys Reserve, for I am Sure Lord Hartn likes Londesburgh so well, that he would have it upon yr own terms - I hope he won't hire this other house, as he talk'd of, & for a term of Years - here there was a dead Stop, - with only an Ejaculation now & then, of, it is very odd! - I can't make Speeches, - & such kind of no-meaning Words! in short how this will work I can't say - but if she intends as she ought - this will open her Mouth & heart im~ediatly, if Not - I shall be angry, amaz'd and disappointed - Yr Cloaths have been
three Days with ye Tailor, I flatter Myself You'll like them; Mrs G- send her Duty &
I am My Lord Yr Lordship's Most faithfull & most
D Garrick.
I am going to play Macbeth, & have wrote so unintelligibly that I fear you won't make it out - Yr Lordp will Excuse Me.
Febry 26th 1756

I should not have troubled Your Grace so soon again, had not one part of ye last Letter I had ye honor & pleasure to receive, requir'd an immediate Answer - My Wife had a very good opportunity ye last time she was at Chiswick, of telling her Ladp that I had ventur'd to write to Yr Grace in favor of Dr Boyce, & that I had receiv'd an Answer, yt You would not oppose him - I thought this proper to be told as Yr Lordp hinted in yr last; that Letter & one I wrote upon a late melancholly Occasion, (I think) may be all wch shd be own'd; tho her Ladp will scarcely demand a Confession, but whatever is thought right, We shall acquiesce in - there is such an unaccountable Suspicion & Jealousy in Every Word, Action & Look, that it behoves all Persons concern'd to be extreamly Wary - Mrs Garrick continues in favor, & was this day honor'd with ye Six Duns to Hampton & returns to Chiswick to Dinner - Her Ladp
even sent a Slice of Pleasantry to Me with a Loin of Chiswick Pork, wch Madam brought home from thence - the Tail of ye Pig was not cut off, but sent wth ye Loin, & she desir'd that I would put it to my Wig, & parade with it in Hyde Park - Her Bosom Friend has left off Tails - I mean to her hair, & now rides out in a Bag - indeed it is time - Poor Miss Anderson is much, very Much to be pitied; My Wife is Melancholly about her - a Day or two ago Dr Hoadly (ye Divine) breakfasted wth Me, & among other Things I ask'd whether a piece of News wch I had accidentally heard was true, that his Father & ye Duke of Devonshire had some misunderstanding - upon which he told me his Father's Tale, & indeed a most Spiritual one it was, truly Ecclesiastical from top to bottom - I could not help from his own Account to Argue with him, & hint, that ye Arguments were rather those of an Attorney than a Bishop - He likewise seem'd to say, that yr Grace was satisfy'd, which I would not contradict, & that Mr Lowth, was not displeas'd with his Father's behavior - this perhaps was only said to soften ye Edges of my impetuosity - I din'd Some time ago with Several Gentlemen, among wch were no less than Six Members of Parliament, chiefly of ye Minority, & by ye turn of their discourse I could gather, that they have warm Expectations of yr Grace's Sanction, I took no Notice at all, but was somewhat surpriz'd, & thought I wd mention it - That yr Grace may still Continue the Darling & Blessing of ye People where You are & that You may soon return safe & well to this Kingdom is ye most Zealous Wish
of Yr most devoted
D: Garrick
My Lord.

Since I finish'd my Letter Mrs G is return'd from Chiswick, & had an Opportunity of hearing from poor Miss A- (for she is watch'd like a Spy) how cruelly she has been Us'd - indeed so cruelly, that, She cannot bear ye Persecution any longer, & is resolv'd to leave 'Em Soon - She is deny'd ye Use of Books, newspapers & Even to speak to ye little ones; They will not suffer her to go into my Lady's Room after Coffee & Tea, but they lock her out, & if by chance she gets in, they return to ye Dining Room; so that now, she is wholly, except at dinner, confin'd to her own Room - she looks terribly - & is told continually of her being Ugly, & that from her Starring, they are affraid she will be Mad, like Others of ye Family; in Short Every shocking thing that can be conceiv'd is Utter'd. this she has open'd this Morng to my Wife with floods of Tears;
nay her Lp wants to set Mrs G- against her & has told her, that Miss A- rails at her & Me & often abuses Us - their Rancour Ev'n runs into Such foolish improbable Extreams - thus ye Poor Sweet-temper'd Creature scarcely Lives, but can indure it no longer -

I make no doubt but Endeavors will be made to Set Yr Grace against her, but be assur'd she is a most Worthy & truly virtuous Woman & much unfit for her present Society - This I thought not improper to inform Yr Grace of, & indeed my Wife beg'd that I would - who desires her Duty & respects.
March 20th 1756
My Lord.

I had the honour of Yr Grace's last Letter three Days ago; and as her Lp's Health is the subject of one part of it, I would not delay any longer sending the best Intelligence I could about it - Had Mrs Garrick been in ye least apprehensive of Danger from that Quarter, I should have immediatly appriz'd yr Grace of it, but notwithstanding Mr Arundel's Letter, wch to be sure was written by her Direction, He must know that it was only a Scene of ye Old Farce: We were allarm'd one Morning by Ly Francis sending to my Wife, to go & see her Lp who was taken ill, Mrs G. could not go that Morng; but Ly Rachael Walpole & Ly Francis did, & when they had got near Chiswick, behold they met her Lp going to Town, as well as could be Wish'd; Some little Grumbling's there have been since, & keeping her Bed Chamber, but be assur'd there is Nothing that ought to allarm Yr Grace - I cannot Express to You, the inward Joy & Satisfaction I feel, at the Unexpected Situation of Affairs in Ireland; It appears to Me (who know the People a little) like a Golden Dream; this Success of Yr Grace is ye Topic & admiration of Every Body, & this alone, all Parties here unite to applaud & rejoice in - may no unlucky Circumstance arise to cloud this delightfull prospect! I am not in ye least apprehensive of it, but from my Soul I wish Your Grace in England again,
and happy in the Reflection that you have done, what ye Wisest and most Zealous imagin'd almost an Impossibility.
The Politicians & News papers have Settled Matters for Yr Grace already, but as they have join'd some improbalities with it, I have not given ye least Credit to it.

Miss Anderson has left Chiswick & gone to Lady Molineux's - She is to see My Wife on Monday, & I am affraid has a most lamentable Tale to unfold - Mrs Garrick durst not converse with her much at Chiswick . there were such Jealousies & watchings; - Miss A's Heart was almost broken, & she told Mrs Garrick, that she could Endure it, no longer; my Wife would give no advice, but is very glad that she has left them; Upon my Word the Usage of this good Creature, is not to be believ'd: Miss Mostyn endeavour'd to quarrel several times wth her, in order that some story might be told of her Behavior to my Lady, to hurt her Elsewhere - This Scheme has been try'd wth regard to Me, but I am as insensible to her Wickedness, as her heart is to goodness, and did not other Considerations strike upon my Mind, I should absolutely forget that such strange unheard of Creatures were in Being - Your Grace may be Assur'd that I shall be must punctually discreet about poor Miss A- when I see her, I shall pour some balm upon her Wounds, & desire her not to imagine that any unjust representations of her, will Ever Effect her wth Yr Grace - I was frighten'd most Extreamly two Days ago, Mrs Gk was taken ill at Hampton & very much so, I brought her very ill to Town, but Dr Taylor in a few hours set us all to right again.
I am Ever & Ever Yr Grace's Most devoted & Obedt
D: Garrick
Monday -
Sir.

I should not have troubled You with this, my last Letter, were it not to Answer that part of Yrs which relates to my Friend Mr
Berenger - He might indeed say, that he knew of my good Intentions towards You, but he scarce could tell You that I had intentions to Serve You in ye Orphan of China , as he knew from ye Nature of ye Affair, that it was impossible - Your Warmth, or Quickness to Err , as you are pleas'd to call it, has hurried You a little too far in that part of yr Lettr, where you talk of Equitable treatment , so I shall leave that to be answer'd by Yr own Feelings, when The Quickness of Seeing yr Error , returns: I have always declar'd that my private Resentments shall never interfere with ye Public Entertainments; & Mr Murphy may be assur'd, tho He should publish twenty Volumes of abuse upon Me, whenever he sends Me a Performance that I think will succeed upon ye Stage, I will certainly perform it in ye best manner I am able, nor will I receive One , on ye Other hand, tho whose only Merit should be, that It's Author has publish'd the same Quantity of Panegyrick upon Me -

The New Acquisition of Mr Derrick wch you are pleas'd to honor me with, is not ye only Mistake in Yr Letter, but that & Yr mention of Shakespear - Voltair Hawkesworth &c are visible proofs of Yr anger but surely not of Yr Wit, Yr Judgment, or Yr Justice.

I am not in ye least surpriz'd, that Your Letter of Yesterday, should be so totally inconsistent with that I receiv'd from You ye Day before - My Acquaintance which You so warmly desir'd in that, & wch I so freely & as Warmly offer'd to You in my Answer, I now as Willingly take again & assure You that it shall not Ever incommode You for ye future.
I am Sr Yr most humle Ser
D Garrick
Sepbr 10th 1757
My Lord.

Mrs Garrick & I are very happy that You are pleas'd to Express such confidence of our Taste, but our great desire & Endeavour to
do Nothing that shall displease Yr Grace has induc'd Us to send the Enclos'd - which I must beg to have return'd to Me by ye next Post, that the Embroiderer may finish his Work in Time. We think that ye two pieces of Velvet yt are pin'd togeather will make a most agreeable Mixture; the figur'd Velvet for ye Sleeves & Wastecoat, & ye plain one, for ye Coat; but then to be compleat it must be Embroider'd with Silver, for we fear that Gold will be too heavy - the Single pattern of figur'd Velvet would likewise make waistcoat & Sleeves with ye Plain one, tho not so Gay; or a whole Suit of it Embroider'd with Silver or Gold, would look well - We shall wait for Your Grace's Determination & immediatly go to work -

We would certainly choose ye two pin'd togeather with Silver, & if yr Grace pleases, the Embroiderer would make ye Stalks of ye little flowers in Silver, & put a Spangle into ye Middle of Each little Rose, where there is now a small hole -

There was a Report at Hampton - Yesterday that there was an insurrection in Derbyshire about ye Militia Act, & that Chatsworth was surrounded by ye Mob - We are in hopes that it is a Mistake, for it would be very hard that Yr Grace should have any uneasiness about an Act, which I am persuaded, You could neither project or approve of. Mrs Garrick joins wth Me in Duty and
I am My Lord Yr Grace's most humble, faithful and most Obedient Servant
D Garrick.
PS. pray return ye Patterns.
Hampton Sepbr 14th 1758
My Lord.

I receiv'd Yr Grace's Letter with the Draught for five hundred pounds. I cannot Express how much I think Myself oblig'd to Yr Grace for this new Mark of Yr Kindness to Me; I will take care that such confidence & Bounty shall be return'd by care & punctuality at least on my part - the Mistake about Yr Grace's being in Town was owing to Mr Martin who told Me that he met You going to Kensington, & when I ask'd at Devonshire House, the SubPorter's answer to me, that You was gone to Chatsworth, (wch might imply Yr being in Town ye Day before,) confirm'd Me in it - Nor were Mrs Garrick & I undeceiv'd till the Day before Yesterday, when Mrs Mostyn told my Wife that You had not been in Town at all, but that she had written to desire that Yr Grace would come upon My Lady Burlington's dangerous Relapse - Mrs Garrick attends there Every day, & she assures Me that she never saw so Woeful a Spectacle, & that it is impossible her Ladysp should continue
long in her present melancholly, wretched Condition - My Wife was quite in ye vapors at her Return from Chiswick last Night, & still thinks she cannot possibly hold long as She is - She goes again to day & is resolv'd, if she can, to persuade her to be remov'd from the filth, she is at present in - It is Exactly, by her Account, Dean Swift's Description of the Yahoos - her looks are dreadful & her Shrieks more so - all is not right within! - at Mrs Garrick's going away Mrs Huet call'd her into a room & with tears in her Eyes open'd her heart to her; she has conceiv'd some terrible Notions of a certain Person, & thinks her Ladyp's Actions wholly influenc'd by her - My Wife was indeed struck with some things but she rather persuaded Mrs Huet that she might be mistaken - I was desir'd not to send this to Yr Grace, but I could not forbear it, tho perhaps of very little Consequence - I shall be in London on Monday next & will certainly send the patterns by Tuesday's or Thursday's post to Chatsworth - If any Matter should arise, for Mrs G- is now at Chiswick, I shall certainly trouble Yr Grace with another Letter on Saturday.
I am My Lord Yr Grace's Most humble & most faithfull Sert
D Garrick
Octr 5th 1758
My Lord.

What I have to say to Yr Grace is of little Consequence, & Yet I could not forbear giving You this trouble - Mrs Garrick call'd Yesterday at Chiswick to see ye Young Lords & Lady Dorothy; but they were with ye Dutchess of Devonshire. She saw Mrs Loxley, who enter'd into some particular conversation with her, wch Mrs Garrick thinks Yr Grace shd know - she therefore desires that You will Suspend any Intentions that Your Grace may have, or be Sollicited about, with regard to Lady Burlington's Maids till Mrs Garrick has seen Yr Grace - I know that my violence &
Suspicions are laught at, but indeed I am seldom Violent without some foundation, or Suspicious without a Cause:
- Foul Deeds will rise!
Tho all ye Earth o'erwhelm them &c.

In my return to London last Tuesday, I overtook the shatter'd remains of the Grenadiers & first Battalion of Guards that were so pepper'd at our last Enterprize : I had much talk with Coll Cary & a Captn Williams - They speak very plain & to the purpose. My heart danc'd to hear with what warm praises they Speak of Lord Frederick - He is their Darling - Williams , whom I don't know, swore that if Lord Frederick had commanded the Whole instead of the Company of Grenadiers, they should not have been in such deplorable Circumstances. They don't believe that his Lordship was Ever in ye Sea; & likewise Williams protested to Me, that Genl Dury who has been so much blam'd, was not ye adviser of what prov'd so fatal to them, but that he behav'd, in ye most Noble & Gallant Manner imaginable. He likewise added that he was little known to Genl Dury, but that he thought it his Duty to tell ye truth & more particularly, as he could not justify himself.
Mrs Garrick sends her Duty with mine with our thanks for some very good Venison We receiv'd two Days ago.
I shall pay my Respects at Devonshire house the Moment that I hear Your Grace is in Town.
I am Ever & most faithfully Your Grace's Most dutifull
D Garrick.
Hampton
Dear Sir.
I receiv'd Yr last Lettr in Hampshire, the Evening before I left Portsmouth, or I should most certainly have appointed a Day for ye Pleasure of meeting You at Winchester.
The Liberty you took with Me, I esteem a favor, & I am sorry that I had it not in my Power to see You & my friend, & Dr Hoadly togeather -

I shall wait with Pleasure Your own, or rather Yr Muse's, time, for favouring Me with a sight of ye desart Island , & the Way to Keep him - follow your amusements, & correct at yr Leisure, & my Life for it, we shall neither of us repent ye Consequences - I think myself much honor'd by Mr Domvilles favourable Opinion of Me, I beg that You will pay my Respects to him.

If you think that the Salt Water will abate your dramatic inclinations, I must absolutely prohibit Your drinking it - I most willingly consent to yr catching as many Cods , as you please, but I prescribe no other Use of ye Sea Water to You - Were it really a Remedy for Ev'ry kind of Cacoethes, I could send You a waggon load of Writers (scurvy ones) to be duck'd & drench'd for their own & ye Public Benefit - The Public has done You Justice, & you cannot possibly make a more grateful return, (next to writing Yrself), than by doing yr best Endeavors to cure these Gentlemen -
The Fracas you mention, was a matter of much Concern to me - I despise the attacks & Misrepresentations of Blockwig, but shall be Ever truly Sorry when I am misunderstood by a Man of Genius.
I am Dr Sr Your most Obedt humble Sert
D Garrick.

PS. I was in London the first of Augst but did not flatter Myself that I shd see You - when you return to London, pray let me have a Line from You - any Parcel sent to my house will be with Me here ye next Day.
To Arthur Murphy Esqr to be left with Paul Vaillant Esqr in the Strand, London.
Friday noon Dear Sir,

I have done a little with my pencil, but not enough; and I am not certain that I have done it as it ought to be. You will consider my cuttings, and look upon them merely as marks that the scene is too long, and follow your own judgment, which must be the best in omitting and restoring. The scenes with me and Bashful are much too long: I have taken out some speeches of merit, merely because they were rather inclining to taudry. You will do as you please. - I think that the beginning of the third act, between Mrs. Lovemore and me, had better be spared, for fear it should take from the last act; and there is another reason for rejecting it, and a much stronger one, which is, that I shall never be able to change my dress from top to toe (as I must for Lord Etheridge) while the scene of the Ladies is acting. If I were to dress in the hurry I necessarily must to be ready, I shall be so blown that the following scene will suffer for it. - The fourth act is too long, very near as long as the second by the pages, and with very little curtailing: - I am very much in doubt whether the play would not be better without the circumstances of the buckles; for Sir Brilliant breaks in a little improperly upon Sir Bashful and Lovemore. I think Lady Constant may naturally come upon them after she has torn the letter; and, to me, the scenes will appear more spirited and connected - but this you will determine as you please.

I have some little to say upon the fifth act, which will give you no trouble: I must desire to read that with you, when I come to town next Monday, if agreeable to you. I shall be at the house between twelve and one, and should be glad to see you there; -
if you will bring the four acts as you settle them, we may go immediately to work. - As the fifth act stands, there are no less than three different letters produced and read upon the stage; - should not that circumstance, if possible, be avoided? I think a very little alteration will remedy that, and give the conclusion more spirit. I will offer it to your consideration next Monday, if I have the pleasure of seeing you.
Mignionet is now so good a character that I think Mrs. Kennedy should play it, and Mrs. Bradshaw that of Furnish; but those matters I will settle with you on Monday.
If I had been allowed more time, I could have done more; but I was willing to send it, that no time might be lost.
I am, dear Sir, Your most obedient servant, and sincere well-wisher,
D. Garrick.
Sunday, 12 o'clock at night Dear Sir,

I have finished your Comedy this moment, and I must send it away by the coach at six o'clock - so I must be very concise with you. - It is a very pleasant laughing Comedy of business, and will have great effect in the acting, but it must be well taken care of in the getting of it up. My objections are very few and trifling.

I do not quite like the manner of Belinda's fainting in the Park - there is not sufficient cause for it, as it is now managed - however, you may justify it by Moliere: it is equally probable with his scene. - Should Belinda so readily come into her father's proposal of marrying Belmont? - she should have more regard for her friend Clarissa.
The latter end of the last Act is a little too long bringing matters to bear - however, there is so much to be done that you must not cut too deeply neither. - I am half asleep, or I would say more to you - but I thank you for the pleasure I have had; and I most sincerely assure you, that I have the greatest expectations from it. I am, dear Sir,
Your most obliged and obedient servant,
D. Garrick.
To Arthur Murphy, Esquire.
Sepr 17th 1761
Sir

I receiv'd Your Letter as I was stepping into the Chariot to go to Hampton. I desir'd my Brother to call upon You but You was in ye Country - I really cannot answer for any idle Stories that may
circulate about this Town. it has been ask'd Me several times, whether We were to have Your Pieces, & my constant answer has been that I imagin'd We were, for Mr Lacy told Me, that he had Settled with You upon the Terms, that We two had previously talk'd of, & agreed to, in Bushy Park - and he farther assur'd Me that You were well pleas'd with them - I am much Surpriz'd at his proposal of my playing Yates's Character, for he knew my Sentiments upon that Matter.

So it stood between Me & Mr Lacy, and I appeal to You Sir, whether it was not very Natural for Me, to think that We had bargain'd for Your two Pieces. Nay to convince You that I thought so, & that You knew it, I order'd Johnstone to write out some of the Parts, & You forbid him, for some Reason or another - You likewise told Me, that You were preparing a Comedy for Us, The Man does not know his own Mind , & that it should be deliver'd to Me before ye opening of the house, & You told my Brother that You would write to Me about it - But I have neither Seen You, or heard from You, till the Receipt of yr Letter, but have heard from others, that You are in another Interest, which indeed I could not, nor can I now, account for.
I am Sr Your most Obedient Servt
D: Garrick
To Arthur Murphy, Esqr at Lincolns-Inn.
Sir,

To take up as little of your time as I possibly can, I must tell you that Mr. Lacy assured me that he had made a bargain with you
for the two pieces, and that he engaged to see it fulfilled on my part, which he could very well do for the reasons which I told you in my last letter. - As to his saying that I should appear in Mr. Yates's character, there must be some mistake between you, for he denies his having said to you that I would play Yates's part : he told you, in conversation, that All in the Wrong ought to have been acted in the winter, originally with us, and that I should have done Yates's part; but that he made no stipulation for my taking the part upon the revival of the Comedy.

The affair of your new Comedy is wholly in your own hands, and we must acquiesce: the Managers of Drury Lane Theatre have this to say, that you have always settled your own terms with them, and without a single objection on their part: when they have deviated in their agreements with you from the usual compact with authors, it has been at your own request.
What additions you have made to my fortune I am much obliged to you for, and am sorry that you think the Managers have been the only gainers. I am, Sir,
Your most obedient humble servant,
D. Garrick.
Decr 17th 1761
Dear Colman.

I rejoice that you are arriv'd safe at Bath, but most sincerely wish you as little pleasure there as possible, and You may guess the Reason - Fitzherbert being with You will, I fear, most powerfully counteract my Wishes, however I have some small hopes from his not being under ye same Roof with You -

I have this moment seen our Friend Churchill & told him a fine Scheme of Vaughn's in conjunction with the Gang of Pottinger - they are going to publish a Set of Papers call'd the Genius , in order to forestall Yrs & deceive the Public It is a most infamous design, & I desir'd Churchill would Let Thornton know of it, which he will do immediatly, & prevent their Scoundrillity by some humourous Paragraph - If you wd have any thing done, write directly & You shall be obey'd most minutely.

I have read yr last, & think it a fine Plan a little too hastily finish'd. there is Strength, & good Sense, but I want more laugh & pleasantry. our New Tragedy creeps on; We might steal it on to Six Nights with much loss, but, I hope, that the Author will be reasonable, & satisfy'd with what We have already done, without insisting upon our losing more to force a Reputation - this Entre Nous - You have heard I suppose of a Coll Barry , who has taken ye
Lyon by the Beard in ye Parliamt house; Pitt made no Reply to it, & lost his Question - the Town in general think that ye Coll was rather too rough - There will be fine Work anon! - Whitehead's Play has been once read, & has a great deal of Merit -

Pray let me see you soon with yr Bundle of Excellencies - Mr Murphy has at last declar'd off with us, & in a Letter to Obrien says, that he has been so great a loser by ye Managers of Drury Lane that he can never more have any dealings with Us - Wish Me joy my dear Friend, but Keep this to yrSelf for Many Weighty reasons -
My Love to Fitzherbert & believe Me most
Affectionatly Yours
D Garrick
Mrs Garrick prests her Compts to you -
Drury Lane Theatre
half an hour past Six My dear Peter.

If the Sight of my hand writing would give You the Smallest Satisfaction, You should have so Much of it, that there should not be so Satisfy'd a Gentleman in the whole County of Stafford - I have so much Writing, & like it so little, that I never think of troubling You with a Voluntary , & more so, as I am conscious, that Mine, like those of poor old Lamb, (yr late Organist), would only give You a Yawn or two, & End with a Nap.

last Night I had the honour of Some Litchfieldians to Sup with Me, who stay'd till near two this Morning. All good men & true - viz - Levett, Sudall Dick Bailye, the two Robinsons, & two Garricks - to which were join'd the facetious Author of the Jealous Wife , (my particular friend Colman) & Dr Douglas Chaplain to the Earl of Bath, & tho I was in some allarm all ye Night on Account of a few Symptomatic Creepings about my Kidneys, yet we were very chearfull, tho not roaring - I have undergone a terrible hour & a half three Weeks ago, & now am taking Soap by ye Pound, & Lime water by ye Gallon by way of prevention.

We don't despair of Seeing You here this Season, for yr Partner Dick will return soon Enough to You, to give you time to make Us a Visit - if so be as how, Your Inclination tally with ours, & you can please stop yr Ears against ye Lichfield Syrens, who will hold You, & have held You so fast, that a poor Relation can't have a Slice of You to be plain & Serious - George & I have always open Arms & Hearts to receive You - Not but I must hint to You, by ye bye, that if you won't see us this Year, let me beseech You not to make it so late the Next, for our Benefits begin in a Month, & then adieu to all ye Pleasures of ye Theatre.

The King has most graciously renew'd ye Patent for Me, & I, as Graciously, have given the Same Advantages to Lacy, as I have Myself, tho I was desir'd to think how I might be particularly favour'd in the Grant -

I am now Writing, during the first Act of a New Comedy, call'd the School for Lovers - I have Spoke the Prologue, & don't appear in ye Play till the beginning of the 2d when Sr John Dorilant (that's ye Name) makes his Entrance - and a fine, polite, Sentimental, Windling Son of a Bitch it is - a great favourite of ye Ladies, &
much admir'd by the Clergy, & the Aldermen & Common Council of the City of London - Humbug for Nine Nights - Your singing Boy is to go into training, & may turn out well - We are much oblig'd to you for Your attention to us - Dick Bailye has Sent me ye inclos'd Letter for You, & my Brother George backd by the Crowing of the Prompter summons me away - So, my dear Brother, I shall quit you in ye Words of Hamlet
Your most affecte Brother
D Garrick
Chatsworth
July 7th 1763
Dear Peter

We arriv'd here Monday last; George I suppose gave you an Account of our Setting out from London - His Grace of Devonshire desires Me to tell You that he expects to See You at Chatsworth, I will tell
You his own Words - 'let Your Brother know Mr David that he must ride to us, in his worse Coat, put his better into ye Portmanteau & make the best of his way to Chatsworth,' in short You have a warm invitation & will come I suppose if not inconvenient to You, I have some thoughts of seeing You at Lichfield in my return from hence & calling at Lord Vernon's to Dinner only, for I have my Wife, a Friend, (who is acquainted with his Lordp Mr Hubert by name), and my two little Dogs - the Duke will be very glad to See Mr & Mrs Docksey here, if agreeable to them - will You be so good to let 'Em know as much, & that I should have certainly call'd upon 'Em at Mr Seward's, where I heard they were, but was told by a Mr Simpson, that they went from him, the same day I arriv'd here -
I am Dear Peter most Affecly Yours
D: Garrick
PS We have much laugh & all kind of Liberty - Mr Quin is here & in full Spirits.
To Peter Garrick Esqr at Lichfield (turn at Manchester).
Chatsworth
July 9th 1763
Dear Peter.

I wrote to you a few Days ago from this place, informing you that the Duke of Devonshire desir'd to see You here with your better Coat in yr Portmanteau; & I likewise beg'd of You to let my Brother Docksey know that He & his Wife would be wellcome at Chatsworth, without running ye least risque of having his principles debauch'd - Since I wrote to You my first Letter, I have receiv'd a Letter from Brother George, who, I find, intends being with You very soon - if You both can spare a Day or two
from your Lichfield Friends, the Duke will be glad to See You, You will be both at your liberty to do what you please, & to go when you please - I must tell You that we shall go to Chesterfield Races next Wednesday Sen'night , & Fryday Sen'night , so I hope if you come, it will be before that time, for I don't know how soon after that, I shall be thinking of going towards London; I likewise think to take Lichfield in my way, to see what other Sconces You want in Yr Vicar's Hall, for I am told there is yet a deficiency, which I shall most willingly Supply - I write with his Grace at my Elbow, laughing at Me & jogging me, so excuse my Scrawl - pray come soon, or send me a proper Excuse to Shew his Grace - we have with Us Mr Fitzherbert, Mr Hubert, Mr Quin, &c &c - all in Spirits - Mrs Garrick joins with me in love to You & Sister & I am
Dear Peter Yrs most affecly
D Garrick
July 10th 1763
Dear Colman.
Many thanks to you for Terrae filius - it is very lively, & I long to see ye second Number -

Pray write to me, & let me know how ye Town speaks of our Friend Churchill's Epistle - it is ye most bloody performance that has been publish'd in my time - I am very desirous to know the opinion of People, for I am really much, very much hurt at it - his description of his Age & infirmities is surely too shocking & barbarous - is Hogarth really ill, or does he meditate revenge? - Every article of news about these matters will be most agreeable to me - pray write me a heap of stuff for I cannot be Easy till I know all about Churchill, Hogarth, &c - how did ye Terrae filius work at Oxford?
have you yet receiv'd any Letter from Lord Bath? pray be particular in that ; for tho my Curiosity is much concern'd in my former Questions, my heart & Soul are interested in ye last -
Yrs Ever my Dear Colman
D. Garrick
Mrs Garrick presents her respects to you - All ye News -
My dear Colman.

Tho I have said in George's Letter that I would not write to you till I got to Lyons, yet I can't help scribbling to you, for indeed my dearest friend there is no Love lost between us - I am vastly happy that Powel strikes you so much in the Rehearsal - He will surprize,
& I most cordially wish it, for I think him a very worthy man - pray take care that the Play is quite ready before He makes his appearance.

You can't imagine, my dear Colman, what honours I have receiv'd from all kind of People here - the Nobles & the Litterati have made so much of Me that I am quite asham'd of opening my heart Ev'n to You. Marmontel has wrote me ye most flattering Letter upon our supping togeather, I was in Spirits & so was the Clairon , who sup'd with us at Mr Neville's - She got up to set me a going & spoke something in Racine's Athalie most charmingly - upon which I gave them the Dagger Scene in Macbeth, ye Curse in Lear, & the falling asleep in Sr John Brute, the consequence of which is, that I am now star'd at ye Playhouse, & talk'd of by Gentle & Simple as ye most wonderfull Wonder of Wonders - the first Person I find going to England shall bring you Marmontel's Letter - D'Alembert was one of ye Company & Sings my praises to all ye Authors of the Encyclopedie . I am glad to hear of ye Prologue, if they love to hear me abus'd, they will have great Pleasure this winter, for I am told they have begun already, but I am happy & in Spirits, & shall not read any Newspapers on this Side the Alps - in Many thanks to you for ye trouble you take about ye Invasion , cut as you please - I leave it to you - as for Midsummer Nights , &. I think my presence will be necessary to get it up as it ought - however if you want to, do for ye best - & I'll Ensure It's success - Mr Calcraft's behaviour astonishes me, but I hope Lacy will be firm - pray continue in his good Graces for my Sake.

I believe I forgot to pay a little bill for ye Gazeteers, owing to one Owen , ye bill lay in my Study window, will you discharge it for me, & pay for a pair of Spectacles I bought & forgot at ye optician's (I forgot his name) at Charing Cross: it is on ye left side going down to Whitehall - I hate to be in debt & if you or George will clear me there I shall thank you most sincerely - I am this moment going to see a New piece at ye Italian Comedy, & last Night I saw a new one at ye french Comedy, taken from our Tancred & Sigismunda, it had very indifferent success, but ye Clairon was great; she has her faults (between you & me) but I don't say so here, for she idolizes me -

God bless you my dear Colman, & have a corner of yr Eye upon my theatricals, I think you have begun well & may continue it, if my Partner be advis'd & stick tightly to his Business - he behaves well & I most sincerely wish for all our sakes that he may not want
Me - I have desir'd George to write his next Letter to Florence, pray put in a postscript that I may comfort myself in foreign parts with ye sight of yr most agreeable scrawl - once more my worthy Friend Adieu! - My Wife sends her Love to you de bon Coeur -
Ever & Ever Yours & Yours
D: Garrick
George has my direction to Florence
to George Colman, Esqr of Lincolns-Inn, London.
Turin
Octr the 18th 1763
My dear Colman.

I wrote last to George & now for You - We got to this pretty City (for it is no better) last Fryday Night, & are oblig'd much against
our wills to stay here till next Saturday, for the Perch of our carriage was broke upon the top of Mount Cenis, by the carlessness of our Voiturier , who instead of carrying it upon ye backs of Mules (as he ought) had it drag'd up that wonderfule Mountain by 12 Men, & it is a great Miracle that it was not dash'd into ten thousand pieces: however We are well contented, & happy, & are resolv'd to fret at Nothing - Mr Pitt, & all ye English here, are most particularly kind to Us - this Day a Gentleman shew'd me two London Chronicles in which they have abus'd Me most clumsily; I read their Malignity with as much sang froid as Plato himself would have done, tho, Entre Nous , I wish they had not mention'd a certain Duke, but he too is above feeling their Nonsense - I cannot but take Notice that Mr Straughn has twice officously excus'd himself for the abuse upon Me in his Paper, has sworn as often that there shd be no more of it, & has as often treacherously broke his word - but I am neither amaz'd or uneasy at it, & so you may tell our Friend Becket.

We have nothing here in our way, but a miserable Bouffi Opera, & ye worst dancing I Ever saw - the People in ye Pitt & Boxes talk all ye while as in a Coffee house, & ye Performers are Even with 'Em, for they are very little attentive, laugh & talk to one another, pick their Noses, & while they are unEngag'd in Singing, they walk up to ye Stage Boxes, (in which the other Actors & dancers sit dress'd in Sight of ye Audience) turn their backs, & join in ye laugh & Conversation of their Brethren, without ye least decency or regard to ye Audience; I never was more astonish'd in my life; their Theatres are very Elegant, the whole is compos'd of Pit & Boxes (five or six rows of Em) without Galleries - Each Box is like a little room where they receive visitors, & think & talk of Every thing but what passes upon ye Stage - I forgot to tell you that we had the finest day imaginable for passing ye terrible Mount Cenis - I was highly Entertain'd indeed, & it is much more inconceivable, (I mean the manner of ascending & descending) than it is dangerous or Disagreeable. I long to hear from You or George, I am sorry that I did not desire a Letter to this place, it would have reach'd me by this time, & I shall not be at Florence this fortnight at least, so You must not be surpriz'd that You have not an Answer to any thing may be sent there. remember that I address myself to both of You - all letters for ye future must be directed for Me to ye Marquis Belloni at Rome , till I send to ye Contrary - the travelling through Savoy & Piedmont to this City is the most romantick & delightfull with regard to the Scenery, that can be imagin'd, but the Nastiness in
ye Inns, the peculiarity of Nastiness, is likewise as much above conception - I have taken some Memorandums of the things which I have seen with my own Eyes, that exceed all belief, & which I shall write down very soon, & send to our friend Townley as a Nosegay for You & Schomberg - pray make a Hollyday on purpose, & let it be read in full assembly over a bottle of ye Dr's Claret by that aforesaid Arch-Blackguard the revd Mr James Townley. Write to me soon I beg of You - let me know Every thing, but most particularly what concerns Yourself, for yt (if good) will be most wellcome to me. I write in haste but from ye heart -

My fellow traveller Mence is oblig'd to go off for Minorca. We shall part in a few days, he to his Regiment & I for Florence : My wife has been very ill & frighten'd us all - but She is now well & herself again - she desires her Love to You & George - pray remember Us to the Huberts, Churchill, Schomberg, Drs Hay & Smalebroke & all whom you know, I wd remember, if I could. God bless You my dear dear Friend
Ever & most affectionatly Yours
D Garrick
PS. Our duty pray to Lord Bath.
To George Colman Esqr in the new Square, Lincolns-Inn at London.
Florence Novr 30th 1763
My Lord

I had Your Grace's very flattering Commands to give You some Account of our proceedings when we got into Italy: We have hitherto met with no disagreable Accident but the breaking the Perch of our Coach upon Mount Cenis; which retarded us some Days at Turin, where Mr Pitt confer'd all kind of Favours upon Us: from thence we went to Milan, and should I recount to Your Grace the honour I receiv'd from Count Firmian, the first Nobleman in the administration there, You would think, as You Us'd to say to me, that all my Geese were Swans: I had no Letter of recommendation to him, but his Servants were Enquiring after Me long before I came, & when I was there, there was no Civility that I did not receive from him; I cannot forbear Acquainting Your Grace with this Circumstance, as it made my Stay at Milan so very agreeable to Me: Count Firmian understands English, has read most of our best Authors; has an unaffected regard for the English Nation, and joins the Strongest Sense to the most Elegant Manners. from Milan We went to Genoa, which struck us more from its situation than any place we had seen before, the fine weather and the persuasion of many People, determin'd Us to sail part of our way to Leghorn in a Felucca; We were two Days and a Night upon the Mediterranean, & Mrs Garrick & Biddy were very much disorderd by the Voyage, We rested three Days at Leghorn Were well feasted by ye Merchants, & have been Ever since feasting upon Virtu` in the Gallery & in the Pallaces of this Place. I have found great preparations making for the Duke of York at Genoa, Leghorn and Florence, but as yet there is no certainty where he is - We shall set forward for Rome to Morrow; the English here are all agreeable, & hold their Conversations in our Appartment (& we have a most magnificent one upon the banks of ye Arno) almost Every Night; there is one Mr Kaye among them, who is known to yr Grace, & is beat constantly by Mrs Garrick at Chess.

Lord Fordwick is still here, but assures Me that he shall soon go to England; I wish that it may be as soon as his Friends desire, & sooner, than his inclinations seem at present willing to agree to - Mrs Garrick presents her Duty to Your Grace & to Lady Dorothy,
We have seen a Picture so Exactly like her Ladyship that we have visited it several times -
I am astonish'd at the profusion of fine things We meet with in Every part of this City, & at the poverty of the inhabitants; they are a new Set of beings to Me, & quite a new Study -

I shall trouble Your Grace no more at present; before I leave Naples, I shall pay my Duty again, & hope in the mean time, that my Brother will be Able to tell me that Your Grace is quite Establish'd in Your health.
I am My Lord Your Grace's Most Obedient & most faithfull humble Servant
D: Garrick
I beg that Your Grace will present our Respects to Lord Frederick, Lord George & My great antagonist Lord John.
Naples
My dear Colman

Per varios casus we are at last arriv'd at our Journey's End - and a very long one it has been - I have now time to shake my feathers a little, & open my heart to thee, thou best of friends - ! We got to this place the 17th, after a most disagreeable Journey from Rome, for we were taken in ye midst of ye heavy rains here, and were well soak'd with them all the Way - at present the weather is inconceivably fine, & we are basking ourselves in a warm sun with the Mediterranean at our feet, and Mount Vesuvius in our view - tho it is Xmas, we have green Peas Every day, & dine with our Windows open - these are our Pleasures in part, as for our distresses, wch have been as ridiculous as unexpected since we left Rome & are the common occurrences upon this Road, I shall reserve them for our social hours at Hampton - We are all at this moment, Biddy not excepted, in the highest Spirits, & I am much ye better for my Expedition: My Lady Orford, who is settled here & has the greatest Interest with ye first People, has been most uncommonly kind to us - I am to have ye honour & Satisfaction of Seeing the King's Italian Actors perform before him in ye Palace, which is a most extraordinary favour; they perform Extempore, & ye Nobleman, who stands in the place of ye Lord Chamberlain, has sent me word, that if I will write down any dramatic Fable & give ye Argument only of ye Scenes, in 24 hours after, they shall play it before Me as ye greatest Compt they can pay Me - I shall work at it to morrow - I hear there is one great Genius among the Performers - the Situation and Climate of this place are most extraordinary, & the People are still more so; they are a new race of beings, & I have the highest Entertainment in going amongst them, & observing their Characters from ye highest to ye lowest - I was last Night at their great Theatre, which is a most Magnificent one indeed; I was really astonish'd at first coming into it - it was quite full, & well lighted up - but it is too great, & the Singers were Scarcely heard - the famous Gabrielli pleas'd me much; she has a good person, is ye best Actress I ever saw on an Opera Stage, & has ye most agreeable voice I ever heard; she sings more to ye ear, than to ye heart - before I left Florence I had much Conversation with an old Servant of Yr Father's, who lives wth Sr Horace Mann - he remembers
your being born, & shew'd me ye house where you first wawl'd & cry'd , I look'd at it for ten minutes with pleasure - I need not tell you how well I am prepar'd to set you right, if you shd hereafter make any mistakes about your Age, & I fear that we already differ a year or two in our Calculation - I cannot quit you, till I say something about Rome: I hardly slept the night before I arriv'd there with ye thoughts of seeing it - my heart beat high, my imagination expanded itself, & my Eyes flash'd again, as I drew near the Porta del Popolo ; but the moment I enter'd it, I fell at once from my Airy Vision & Utopian Ideas into a very dirty ill looking place , (as they call it) with three crooked streets in front, terminated indeed at this End with two tolerable Churches - wt a disappointment! my Spirits sunk & it was wth reluctance that I was drag'd in the afternoon to see the Pantheon - but my God, wt was my Pleasure & Surprize! - I never felt so much in my life as when I Entered that glorious Structure: I gap'd, but could not speak for 5 Minutes - It is so very noble, that it has not been in ye Power of Modern Frippery, or Popery (for it is a Church you know) to extinguish Its grandeur & Elegance - Here I began to think myself in Old Rome, & when I saw the ruins of the famous amphitheatre -

Omnis Caesareo cedat labor Amphitheatro - I then felt my own littleness - & was convinc'd that the Romans were as much superiour to the Moderns in Every thing, as Vespasian's Amphitheatre was to Broughton's - it is impossible, my dear Colman, to have any Idea of these things from any Prints that have been made of 'Em, - all modern performances look better upon paper, but these Ruins are not to be conceiv'd, but by ye sensible & true Avouch of your own Eyes . Tho I am pleas'd, much pleas'd with Naples, I have such a thirst to return to Rome, as cannot possibly be slak'd till I have drank up half ye Tiber, which, in it's present state, is but a scurvy draught neither. it is very strange that so much good poetry shd be thrown away upon such a pitiful River; it is no more Comparable to our Thames, than our modern Poets are to their Virgils & Horaces - I was so taken up for ye fortnight I was at Rome in seeing ruins, Statues Pictures & Palaces, that I had not ye least inclination to see his Holiness, & his troop of Cardinals, tho they had two or three publick days when I was there - I shall have their blessings in ye holy Week. I attend Lord & Lady Spencer to morrow to Herculaneum , where, I am told, they have dug up Every Utensil that were in use among ye Romans, & have got ev'n a Lady's Toilette Entire - the Lady herself was found dressing herself & in
ye act of sticking a bodkin into her hair; which bodkin is of a most Elegant make, not much unlike a Modern one, with ye difference of a Jupiter or Minerva carv'd at ye End of it: next week we shall mount to see ye top of Vesuvius ; it is a most terrible Object indeed, & ye greatest Natural wonder I Ever yet saw - in short we are Encompass'd with classical prodigies & when we shall be able to get out of this Enchanting Circle, I cannot possibly tell - I shall write the next post to Brother George, from whom I expect a letter very soon - tho I receiv'd one from him, and another from You at Rome - direct your next, as I desir'd before, A Monsieur Monsieur Francesco Barazzi Banquier a Rome - or rather, to Me chez Monsr Frano Barazzi &c . - I have seen ye St James's Chronicle : here, & from thence & other papers, I see that the Deuce is in him goes on as my heart could wish - I have seen letters, where King is much prais'd & Miss Plym - but surely O'Brien & Pope must bear ye belle. the poor Mids. Night's Dream I find has fail'd by a Letter in ye Chronle: - I know ye Author & love him tho he abuses the Grown Gentlemen & ladies -

Mrs Cibber, I find, is still prudent, & will run no risques of reputation to support poor Old Drury, to whom she has many, many obligations - What is become of ye Invasion , ye Dupe , & ye new Entertainment ; I hope I shall have some account of 'Em, & a good one, in your next. how does Powell go on? - does he keep or lose his ground - if he is to be advis'd don't let him play ye fool, as others have done; remember me to all of them, that you think deserve my remembrance; send me some News dear Colman as soon as you receive this - my Love to George - I have not yet receiv'd his letter to Florence: If Clutterbuck is among you my best affections to him too, & thank him for his delightfull letter & tell him I hope to have ye solid pudding instead of ye praise - I think hitherto that my Plan of Operations have been as nearly follow'd, as ye Circumstances wd admit of, so that be ye success good or bad, I have my share of ye praise as well as of ye pudding - that for Clutterbuck - pray desire George to let me know how David & all his Children are (particularly) in his next - My Wife sends her Love to Him & You & Clutterbuck ; Your Story of Hubert & his family have not surpriz'd me, as we rec'd a Letter from Mrs Hubert & one from Castlefranc: there never sure was such a mean Scoundrel - He had no way to Excuse the meanness of his behaviour to us by pretending a falsehood - I was an Entire Stranger to ye whole, upon my honour, so that it is impossible my Wife could suspect
yt her Jewels were chang'd without acquainting me with it - proof positive - Mrs Hubert might have spar'd herself ye trouble of sending such a letter after Mrs Garrick to Florence, & she will be sorry that she writ it when she knows ye truth, as I suppose she may before this - What is become of my friend Garnier? - if he's in London pray my Love to Him, we could wish to meet him in Italy, I fear that he will set out next Spring, & then we shall not see him, as our intentions are to go through Germany from Venice, & so by Brussels, & not return to Paris - pray let me know his Motions - What is become of your Terence? I have not yet wrote a word of ye 4th or 5th of the Clandestine Marriage , but I am thinking much about it - We are made so much of (as Mr Cadwallader) by your Dukes & Earls & Barons & Baronets, that I have not a moment for thinking - Churchill's affair makes me unhappy - what are you doing with Wilkes? - is not he undone? or will they go too far , & give him once again ye advantage? - & wt will he do with it when he has it? - My heart overflows to Schomberg, Townley, Hubert & I am
Ever & most affecty thine my dear friend
D Garrick

P.S. I have in my hurry forgot this blank side but you can make it out - my Wife & I desire you'll present our Respects to Lord Bath - I do assure You if the Juice was in him , I should not be so Easy with the flirtation that his Lordship sends, & Mrs Garrick receives so warmly, however I am in a Country yt will teach me how to secure my honour under lock & key, & I hope to return to England with less apprehensions of his Lordship - my best wishes to Mr Burney I shall write soon to him. A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman in Lincolns-Inn a Londres, Ingleterra.
Naples
My dear George.

I wrote last Week to my friend Colman, & since that I have receiv'd his most friendly & agreable packet - I rejoice most sincerely with him at ye Success of the Deuce is in him , & am happy that his benefit turn'd out so Well without my assistance; had I been in England he should have met with no Obstructions in a certain affair, & I hope that he will have philosophy enough to go through those bad roads patiently for a few Months more, which I have labour'd thro' for so many years - My love to him, & all that belong to him, remember that , for I fear I forgot it in my great hurry, & multiplicity of Matter - I yesterday receiv'd a very Entertaining letter from our friend Mrs Hale ; pray let her know as much, & how delightfull her Corespondence is to Us, & that Mrs Garrick will attack her from this place very soon: We have been here a fortnight, & are as well & as jolly, as a fine Climate, fine things & fine doings can make Us - We dine & sup with Lord Spencer, Lord Exeter, the Minister, Consul, &c &c &c almost Every day & Night, we have balls more than twice a Week & parties innumerable - in short We are made very much of, & I have not once yet (tho we have had crosses upon ye road) wish'd Myself in Southampton Street - I rejoice much at ye Success of Powell ; I hope his head will not be turn'd wth it, & that he will not cease to labour night & day at his profession - I hope too & believe, that Mr Lacy has rewarded him accordingly, you may Answer for Me , pray let it be done handsomely - he has Merit & a family, & will have occasion, for our benevolence - I guess by Colman's letter that Your Season to the 6th of Decr has been tolerable; I long to know how it goes on, & therefore pray write as soon as You have receiv'd this, & I may receive it before I leave Rome, where we expect to be about the latter end of February: I shall write the next post day (this day Sen'night) to Mr Burney, & shall let him know the present State of Musick in Italy; pray present my best Compts to him, & tell him that his 3 vols of Cochin have been of more Use to Me than all my other books put togeather - I have lost a little Memdm he gave me about some Musick for him; pray ask him to put it down in yr next letter - I want much to know how You have gone on wth my good Partner, let me be satisfy'd in yt particular in yr next; &
don't forget to desire Burton to keep an exact list of ye Plays for Me wth ye forces, & all occurences as may happen in ye Course of ye Season, not forgetting the popularity of ye divine Imogen .

Colman will tell you how I have been Entertain'd at Rome, & with what appetite I shall return to it again - the two Dances (Love's Brothers) were very kind & Obliging to us - they are both very ingenious & agreable Men: the Painter is a great Genius, & will do wt he pleases when he goes to London, wch will be ye next Spring, I ought to say this Spring, for it is absolutely more than Spring with us - it is as warm now here, as it is with You in June - it is too hot - nay it is Sultry - My Wife sends her love with mine to You & Your Babes - pray write as soon as You receive this - send me a bit of Every thing - & remember to date Yr letter.
Yours Ever & Ever most Affectionatly
D Garrick
PS. Remember me to Love &c What's become of ye New Pantomime?
A Monsieur, Monsieur Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand, London, Ingleterra .
Naples
Jany ye 31st 1764
My dear George.

We have been here six Weeks & intend to stay till about the 23d of next Month; then We shall return to Rome for a Month or more, then We shall set out for Bologna in our way to Venice , & from thence through Germany in our way to England - this is our intended Route, which I will dispatch wth all convenient speed, but am afraid that I shall not see Your fat face, or kiss ye brawn of it, till ye middle of June - now I am out of yr Clutches I must make a Meal, & a good one, in Italy; I shall never return to it again, & therefore I will make Good Use of my time - We have been very happy here & have receiv'd Every mark of favour from all sorts of People - I Eat & drink too much, & laugh from Morning to Night - our Mirth has been lately damp'd by my poor Wife's keeping her bed & room for many Days, with a most obstinate Rheumatism in her hip - she has been blister'd &c &c & tho she is better, yet still continues lame & Weak. however she hopes to be at A Carnaval Masquerade (which begins next Tuesday), in ye Dress of a lame old Woman; I have scolded & phyz'd about it, but if she can wag, she goes - We are continually with Lady Orford, Lady Spencer, Lord Exeter Lord Palmerstn & the Nobility of ye Country, who have descended from their great pride & Magnificence to honour Us with their Smiles - in short we are in great fashion & I have forgot England & all my trumpery at Drury Lane, I am glad you go on so well; I find by Gastrell's Lettr & ye news papers, that ye Rites of Hecute go on well. I hope that you will bring Murphy's play out, that I may not be troubled with it when I come to England: I don't understand yr affair wth him - pray explain it a little: I have wrote to You from this place & to Colman ; but as my Neapolitan Servant put ye Letters into ye Post We are affraid that he pocketed ye Money & Wip'd his Arse with my Wit & humour - I hope you have seen Mrs Hale's Letter, that yr hard Expressions in yr last , may be somewhat melted down in yr next : I can say Nothing about Powel's Benefit, as I am not able to give my opinion at this distance - I fear for his head , & of course for his heart , if he talks of Consequence , he is undone - What in ye name of Wonder is Hamilton doing in Ireland? - I hear, but can't believe ye strange things they say of him - one word about that pray: - You have said Nothing lately
of Covent Garden? - do they beat You soundly, or is it only a gentle trimming: have Lacy & you been content with a hundred quarrels a Week? - Colman has hurt me with an Account of his behaviour to him - I fear he dislikes him as my friend - What a beast, if it is so - ! tell Colman that I love him more & more, & thank him most cordialy for his fairy tale - it puzzled me much, for I saw it in ye Papers before I rec'd his letter about it - I have almost seen Every curiosity of this place - I was very near wet to ye Skin yesterday in ye Elysian fields at Baiae, & therefore did not Enjoy Julius Casar's Palace, & Tully's Villa so much at my Ease as I could wish - I sent Colman an Acct of his age & ye house he was born in. pray let me know if he has receiv'd it -

I beg one of you will write ye moment you can after ye receipt of this directed to Barazzi at Rome as usual with a whole packet full of News, & the other may write a fortnight after directed to Me, chez Monsieur Udney, Consul de sa Majeste` Britanique, a Venise : I will let You know here or at Rome where You may Write after to Me, for yr letters will be most Acceptable upon ye Road - Lord Exeter sends me ye St James's Chronicle, & the London twice a Week wch Entertains me much. I was very much hurt at ye Nonsense in ye St James's about my dancing with ye Duke of D. pray tell Colman that I think Baldwin us'd me like a Scoundrel to print such a heap of Stuff - Colman, I hope, will receive my Share of that paper for Me, when he receives his own -

I shall write to Mr Burney soon - pray remember me kindly to him - wt is become of his Musical Entertainment. don't be angry that I urg'd ye receiving ye debts I mention'd I thought my absence was ye best time for it, & that you might do then what I could not do when in England: My love to Clutterbuck, Townley & all friends - We send our blessings to yr Children & love to yrself -
Most truly Affectionatly, & Eternally thine
D: Garrick.
A Monsieur, Monsieur George Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand a Londres, Ingleterra .
Rome March the 24th 1764
My Lord

I am now writing in a Room, which was once Your Grace's, & is a proof how much this City has fall'n since Your time, for the same
appartments are now Occupy'd by Your humble Servant - I have not troubled Your Grace with our Misfortunes at Naples, & our Accidents in going to it - Mrs Garrick & I, willing to get to Naples before Night, set out before our Coach (Your Grace knows my impatience) in a Chaise of Lord Exeter's, which broke down in ye Middle of ye Post, in ye Severest Storm of thunder Lightning, & rain that I ever saw - as the Servant was gone before to prepare post horses, I was oblig'd to send my wife in a Calash four Miles with a Strange Man to send me help from ye next town, while I sat cooling my heels in ye Road, & taking Care of the nimble-finger'd Neapolitans - My Philosophy had some tryal I must confess - whether my wife by this Accident caught Cold, or was effected by the Climate of Naples, I can't determine, but soon after her Arrival there, she was Seiz'd wth a Rheumatism in one of her hips, was oblig'd to keep her bed for a fortnight, & is not yet quite recover'd tho it is three Months since she was first Attack'd - this has been a great drawback upon our Pleasures, for tho some Husbands would have rejoic'd to have their Wives tyd by ye leg; yet I must confess that I have been fool Enough to wish her Ev'n at ye top of Vesuvius with Me - I have had an opportunity to consider the Characters of the People of Naples in different lights - I have seen them, happy & very Miserable in ye Space of three Months - the Scarcity of Corn produc'd such dreadfull sights, which I would not but have seen for ye world, & yet my heart sinks at ye very remembrance of them - I cannot say which surpriz'd Me most - their natural Curiositys, the People, or the Government - to give Your Grace one trait of their great Minister, & whom they call the Pitt of the two Sicilies; the Marquis Tennuci is so frightned at thunder, that when it begins to grumble, he puts on a Domino, Hood & all, made of raw Silk which, as it will not receive Electrical matter, he thinks will secure him from the Effects of the Lightning - My Lord Spencer was most dangerously ill at Naples, He is now at Rome & in perfect health, his Lordship & my Lady have been most particularly civil to Us - his last letters from England have put him into ye highest Spirits, & one paragraph in a former one gave me infinite Pleasure - Your Grace was most warmly extoll'd for Yr Speech upon a certain Occasion & as warmly applauded for your whole conduct & candour in that affair - the letter was written by One of the other side, & brought double Weight with it - my theatrical affairs have succeeded so well in my Absence, that I have an opportunity of making more Holydays if I chuse it; my health & Spirits have been
so much improv'd by this recess, that I am almost tempted to repent of my Follies, & be a Merry Andrew no longer - I have lost all relish for the Stage both as Manager and Actor -

I cannot flatter Myself that Your Grace will send me any Commissions to buy Pictures or Statues, for I fear that You will not think my Taste in these Matters (which you always underrated) so improv'd by my travels to place any confidence in it, but if I could be of ye least Service in Italy I shall be better able to give an Account of Myself, than I can do at present - Mrs Garrick presents her Duty to Your Grace & Lady Dorothy & If I should not be too impertinent I would present my Respects to her Ladyship & all their Lordships -

The Duke of York will be here in ye holy Week - Great preparations for his Reception - and it is confidently affirm'd from ye best Authority that he will be presented with some of his Holyness's Virtu`, which occasions much uneasiness.
I am Your Grace's most faithfull & most Obedient humble Servant
D: Garrick.
PS We shall go from hence in about 3 weeks to Venice.
Rome April 11th 1764
My dear Colman.

Tho' I resolv'd in my last letter to George not to trouble You any more till I got to Venice, yet I cannot hold it out so long, but must say a word or two more to You from this Place; which of all Places in the World is the most worth coming to & writing about - to shew You, that I think so, You must know that I am antiquityhunting from Morning to Night & my poor wife drags her lame leg after me: by ye bye she is now much better, & we have hopes of her being able to run away again from Me, if she can meet wth another Captn Caswell; She desires her love to you, & thanks You for writing to Me, as I sure to be always in Spirits for some time after ye receipt of a letter from You: I have not been quite so well here
as at Naples, which is rather extraordinary; whether I fatigu'd myself too much, or whether ye Climate does not suit me so well, I can't say, but I have had some disagreeable nervous fiutterings that made me as grave as an Owl for a few days, but since ye rains have fall'n (& they come down here in Pailfulls) & ye Sun is bright upon us, I have been as frisky as ye poor flys, who were woefully damp'd by ye wet weather, but are now as troublesome & as pert as your humble Servant - His Holyness the Pope is trying by prayers tears & intercessions to avert the Famine which his State is threaten'd with - He has crept up the holy stairs (santa Scala) wch were brought from Jerusalem, he has order'd processions & what not - We are not so bad, as they are at Naples, for there indeed ye Tragedy was deep - I remember some Scenes wth horror, & since we came away, many People have dropt down in ye Street, & been taken away dead, from mere want of food - our Prospect at Venice is rather worse, for we hear that ye Plague has spread as far Trieste, & that they begin to talk of Quarantine in ye Neighbouring States, if so, we shall run ye gauntlet terribly, but we are not dismay'd, & must go thro' with it -

I must thank you again for the trouble & Care you have had about Count Firmian's books - He is very happy at ye Execution of ye Commission, and was highly pleas'd with your sending your own matters to him gratis - it pleas'd me much - I have not seen a St James's Chronicle since ye End of Jany - if I have them I wish you wd desire George to keep them for me to rummage over when I come to England - Mr Baldwin I hear is no friend to our house - a propos - I am very angry with Powell for playing that detestable part of Alexander - Every Genius must despise it, because that, & such fustian-like Stuff, is ye bane of true merit - If a Man can act it well, I mean to please ye People, he has something in him that a good actor shd not have - he might have serv'd Mrs Pritchard, & himself too, in some good natural character: I hate your Roarers - Delane was once a fine Alexander - damn ye Part - I fear 'twill hurt him - but this among ourselves - I was told by a Gentleman who is just come from Sterne , that he is in a very bad way - I hope Becket has stood my Friend in regard to what he ought to have receiv'd for me, some time ago - I had a draught upon him from Sterne for 20 pds Ever since he went abroad - pray hint this to him, but let him not be ungentle wth Sterne - I have sent the plan of a fine Scene & colour'd, among some small things in a little Box of Mr Stanley's of ye Custom-house - it is in several parts & wrote
upon ye back which is 1st 2d &c - I will send a further explanation of it, but any Italian & our Saunderson will understand it - they shd go upon it directly, it will have a fine Effect. Many thanks to you for yr attendance on ye Pantomime - I am sure they wanted help - no more humour than Brickbats - I am affraid that Love in humourous matters carries too much Gut to be Spirited - flip flaps, & great changes without meaning may distil from the head, whose Eyes are half asleep; but humour, my dear Coley, & scenes that shall be all alive alive ho, can only proceed from men of small stature, whose Eyes are Either quite asleep, or quite awake - in short, from Men who laugh heartily, & have small scars at ye Ends of their noses - I am surpriz'd about Murphy, & want to know how he from Mr Lacy - poor Lloyd! & yet I was prepar'd - the death of any one we like don't shock us so much when we have seen them long in a lingring decay - Where is ye bold Churchill? - What a Noble ruin! - when he is quite undone, you shall send him here, & he shall be shewn among ye great fragments of Roman Genius - Magnificent in Ruin! - I have wrote this on purpose to tell you that Voltaire in his Additions a l'Histoire Generale , at page 183 under Usages du Seizieme Siecle , says something about translating Plautus into Verse that will be of use in yr preface to Terence - Speed yr Plow my dr friend. have you thought of the Clandestine Marriage ? I am at it - I must desire you to write to me once more & direct a Monsr Monsr G- Gentilhomme Anglais chez Monsieur Dutens a Turin , & I shall get it by hook or by crook Pray send me all kind of news - a Letter from you will comfort me in bad roads, & thro plague & famine - so write I beg as soon as you receive this - desire George to speak to Mr Stanley about my things in his box - my Love to all the Schombergs, Townleys, Kings, Hogarths, Churchills, Huberts &c. &c
Yrs most affectionately Ever
D G
Davd Garrick
Remember me kindly at home -
A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman in the new Square Lincolns-Inn, London. Inghilterra.
Venice June 6th 1764
My Dear George

Here we are still, and indeed very much against my mind; but that the Physicians here all advise me to return to Padua, in order to try an application of the mud of some Mineral Spring at Abano near that city, which they say is a specific for the Rheumatism and Sciatica: My Wife's lameness has been rather worse here, perhaps owing to the watery situation of this place, but I am much out of spirits about it, and would give the world I was at home - God knows whether she may not be crippled all her life, and therefore nobody must blame me for trying every thing for her cure: we go to Padua in a Day or two and shall see what effect the mud will have in three or four days, if a good one we imagine a fortnight will
do, and then we Shall set forward for England as fast as we can, unless I am prevented by a letter from you at Ausburgh, which I hope you have written, and I shall receive very soon - I have prepar'd a great deal of Music for our Use, I am about engaging some Dancers (a Man and Woman) and will endeavour to send you over a good Violin from Rome, an excellent one - If you should have any thing more to say to me, or if any new occurrence has happen'd, you may write to me at Messrs Selwyn and Foley at Paris and I will direct them how to send it forward to me: If you write don't be longer than a few days after you have receiv'd this - I have drawn upon Clutterbuck this day for one hundred pounds in favour of our consul here Mr Udney - pray my Love to Clutterbuck and tell him this, or my friend Stammer, in his absence. I have had notice of the Florence Wine ship'd from Leghorn in the Raven Captn Alexr Scott, and some essences for Mrs Garrick; pray take care when they come, to pay freight and duty and lodge them ready for our arrival - perhaps we may be there as soon as the wine - according to my bills of lading you must pay four shillings sterling for freight - I'll send you the bills by a gentleman next Saturday - Captn Butler is here, and has given me the Ghost and the farces - I think to send a few books by him he sets out from hence next Saturday.

My Love to all friends, and let me hear from you to Messrs Selwyn and Foley - I shan't go to Paris unless you have sent me other News to Ausburgh; in the mean time our Love to you and yours and believe me
most truly and Affectionately Your's
D. Garrick.
No News from Cibber? What of Yates? -

Last Monday I saw the finest sight my eyes ever beheld, it was the Regate in honour of the King's birth-day, and appear'd to be a dream or a fairy tale realiz'd. I am grown fat, and sleep half the day in a Gondola.
A Monsieur, Monsieur George Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand, London (Inghilterra) .
Abano near Padua June 25th 1764
My Lord.

I had the honour of Yr Grace's letter at Venice, where I was Enjoying the magnificent Entertainments which were given by the State to the Duke of York. The Regate they gave him was all a Dream &
fairy Vision, & more than answer'd our Expectations, tho they were sufficiently rais'd by the various reports; & the great preparations: It is said that this visit of his Royal Highness has cost the State & ye four Noble deputed Venetians, more than a hundred & twenty thousand Sequins. They were very solicitous (indeed too solicitous) to entertain him, for they would have overlaid him with ceremony & their great wigs, had not He broke from them sometimes to prevent suffocation - His Royal Highness has been most gracious to Me - I am greatly oblig'd to Your Grace for the very delicate manner of excusing Yourself about Pictures & Statues, and I am thoroughly convinc'd that it is owing to Your Grace's want of Money , & not to my want of taste, that I have not an immediate commission. I shall execute that of the Prints to the best of my power. I am at this moment in treaty for no less than two Pictures by Tempesto, two Bassans, a Vandyke, a Rubens, a Paul Veronese &c. I have a little money to throw away, & I don't see why I should not be a little ridiculous as well as My betters. Mrs Garrick & I are retir'd to this Place to try the Mud of ye hot springs upon her very disagreeable & obstinate complaint: She has undergone the operation Eight times, & thinks herself the better for it - the People here give such an Account of Its Efficacy, that I have withstood the urgent calls of my Brother, & my own impatience to go to England, in hopes of finding some relief for her, if not a Cure. Should we fail here too, our Journey to England will be as Melancholly as it is long - We are in a very pleasant house, well situated, & built by Palladio - it belongs to a Count Seco, who has most politely lent it to us wth Every Convenience, but that of getting good beef & Mutton, till ye 15th of the next month. the imprudent Step of Lady S. S. has sorely vex'd me; I always thought she had a foolish liking for ye Drama, & ye dramatis personae , but I could not have imagin'd, yt the flesh wd have overpower'd her Spirit, when there was a good understanding to have help'd in the Struggle - 'tis a most deplorable Business indeed!
